title: Bemotrizinol: The New Sunscreen Ingredient That's Been 25 Years in the Making
summary:
After a two-decade drought, the U.S. sunscreen market is getting a major upgrade. The FDA has added bemotrizinol to its list of approved ingredients, marking the first new sunscreen chemical since the early 2000s. Dermatologists are thrilled. 'I think we should all be super excited,' says Dr. Tanya Hathaway of Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center. Bemotrizinol offers superior protection against UVA1 rays, which penetrate deep into the skin and cause photoaging—wrinkles, sagging, and spots. Current U.S. sunscreens primarily block UVB (burning) rays, with limited UVA coverage.

Bemotrizinol is a large molecule, making it less likely to be absorbed into the bloodstream—a common concern with avobenzone and oxybenzone. It's also photostable, meaning it doesn't degrade quickly in sunlight. 'It's too big to squeeze through the skin cells to get down into your bloodstream,' explains Dr. Jennifer Stein of NYU Langone Health. The FDA classifies it as GRASE (generally recognized as safe and effective), a status shared only with zinc oxide and titanium dioxide.

Approved in Europe for over 25 years, bemotrizinol is already used in Japan, Canada, and Australia. Its U.S. approval goes into effect August 9, so products could appear later this summer. This move may also pave the way for other modern sunscreen filters. However, Stein emphasizes that clothing and shade remain crucial: 'The more clothing you're wearing, the less you have to depend on sunscreen.' For those wary of chemicals, mineral sunscreens are still an option, though they can leave a white cast. Bemotrizinol offers a new, effective choice for sun protection.
why_it_matters: Teenagers often spend a lot of time outdoors and are building lifelong skin habits. Having a better sunscreen means it's easier to protect your skin daily without the trade-offs of older formulas — and could lower the cancer risks that show up decades later.

background_read: The U.S. Food and Drug Administration (FDA) categorizes sunscreens as over-the-counter drugs, which is why new ingredients must go through a lengthy safety review process. Before bemotrizinol, the last new sunscreen filter approved in the country was ecamsule in 2006, and the widely used avobenzone was cleared in 1996. In contrast, European regulators, who treat sunscreens as cosmetics, have allowed modern filters — including bemotrizinol (also sold under the name Tinosorb S) — since the late 1990s. This transatlantic gap frustrated American dermatologists for years because ultraviolet radiation is the principal cause of skin cancer and visible skin aging. Fred Hutchinson Cancer Center (a top cancer research institute in Seattle) and NYU Langone Health (a major academic medical center in New York City) are among the institutions whose doctors welcomed the long-delayed approval.

perspectives.perspective: A long-overdue win for consumer health
perspectives.description: Bemotrizinol gives Americans access to a broad-spectrum sunscreen that is more stable and less likely to enter the bloodstream. For outdoor athletes, beachgoers, and anyone concerned about sun safety, it offers a new layer of protection that much of the world already enjoys.

Some people are wary of synthetic chemicals in skincare, especially since words like 'oxybenzone' have sparked safety debates. Even though the FDA classifies bemotrizinol as GRASE, building public trust may take time, and some will stick with mineral sunscreens or clothing alone.

The 25-year delay highlights deep differences in how the U.S. and Europe assess sunscreen ingredients. This approval signals a possible shift in the FDA's approach, which could modernize the American sunscreen market without sacrificing safety.

If bemotrizinol's approval sets a precedent, other modern filters sitting in regulatory limbo could follow, giving consumers more options that feel lighter and offer better protection. Still, dermatologists stress that no sunscreen replaces staying in the shade and covering up during peak UV hours.
